entries.definition: The lowest thermodynamic temperature, 0 K (−273.15 °C).
A species that donates a proton (Brønsted–Lowry) or accepts an electron pair (Lewis).
The energy barrier associated with a reaction; in the Arrhenius equation it determines the temperature dependence of the rate constant.
The amount of product actually obtained in a chemical reaction.
Accumulation of molecules, atoms or ions at a surface.
An organic compound in which a hydroxyl group (–OH) is attached to a saturated carbon atom.
An organic compound containing a terminal –CHO group.
A water-soluble base that increases the hydroxide ion concentration in water.
A saturated acyclic hydrocarbon with general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
A hydrocarbon containing a carbon–carbon double bond.
A hydrocarbon containing a carbon–carbon triple bond.
A different structural form of an element in the same physical state, such as graphite and diamond.
A material containing a metal and one or more other elements.
A solid lacking long-range periodic structural order.
A negatively charged ion.
Variation of a physical property with direction.
The electrode at which oxidation occurs.
A solution in which water is the solvent.
The smallest unit of an element retaining its chemical identity.
A spectrum showing wavelengths absorbed by gaseous atoms, often as dark lines against a continuous background.
A spectrum of characteristic wavelengths emitted by excited atoms as they move to lower energy states.
The number of protons in an atomic nucleus, denoted Z.
A measure of atomic size, defined by conventions such as covalent or metallic radius.
The rule that electrons generally occupy available orbitals in order of increasing energy in a ground-state atom.
The change in reaction extent or appropriately normalized concentration divided by the elapsed time.
Exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ mol⁻¹; the number of specified entities per mole.
Equal volumes of ideal gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of particles.
The orbital angular momentum quantum number, ℓ, which identifies a subshell and relates to orbital shape.
Hydrogen spectral transitions ending at n = 2; several lines lie in the visible region.
A species that accepts a proton or donates an electron pair.
Temperature at which the vapour pressure of a liquid equals the external pressure.
Energy required to break a bond; mean bond enthalpy is averaged over specified gaseous bonds.
A measure of bonding between two atoms; commonly 1, 2 or 3 for single, double or triple bonds.
For a fixed amount of ideal gas at constant temperature, PV is constant.
Infrared hydrogen spectral transitions ending at n = 4.
Acids donate protons and bases accept protons.
A solution that resists pH changes upon addition of small amounts of acid or base.
An organic compound containing the –COOH group.
A substance that increases reaction rate without being consumed overall or changing the equilibrium constant.
The electrode at which reduction occurs.
Streams of electrons emitted from a cathode in a discharge tube.
A positively charged ion.
For a fixed amount of ideal gas at constant pressure, volume is proportional to absolute temperature.
An attractive interaction that holds atoms or ions together in a chemical structure.
A symbolic representation of a reaction showing reactants and products.
A dynamic state in which forward and reverse reaction rates are equal.
Separation based on differing distributions of components between stationary and mobile phases.
Solution properties that, in the ideal dilute limit, depend on the number of dissolved particles rather than their identity.
A reaction with an oxidant, commonly oxygen, that releases energy.
Suppression of ionization or solubility of an electrolyte by addition of an ion already present in its equilibrium.
A pure substance made of two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions.
Amount of a component relative to a specified amount or volume of mixture.
Conversion of vapour to liquid; also a class of reactions forming larger molecules with loss of a small molecule.
The species formed when a base accepts a proton.
The species formed when an acid loses a proton.
A bond involving shared electron density between atoms.
Crystals in which atoms form an extended network of covalent bonds.
Half the internuclear distance in a homonuclear covalent bond of a specified type.
Temperature above which a gas cannot be liquefied by pressure alone.
A solid with long-range ordered arrangement of its constituent particles.
A regular three-dimensional array of points describing translational symmetry in a crystal.
Formation of crystals from a solution, melt or vapour; often used for purification.
The total pressure of an ideal gas mixture equals the sum of its partial pressures.
Mass per unit volume, ρ = m/V.
Direct conversion of a gas into a solid.
Spontaneous spreading and mixing of gases due to random molecular motion.
Decreasing the concentration of a solution, usually by adding solvent.
A separation of positive and negative charge.
A vector measure of charge separation; for two point charges its magnitude is charge times separation.
Interactions between permanent electric dipoles of polar molecules.
A tube containing gas at low pressure and electrodes used to produce an electrical discharge.
Separation by vaporization followed by condensation, using differences in volatility.
Escape of gas through a tiny opening under conditions where collisions in the opening are negligible.
A device in which redox reactions generate electrical energy or are driven by it.
Potential associated with an electrode relative to a reference electrode.
Use of electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous chemical reaction.
A substance that produces mobile ions in solution or in the molten state.
Transport of electric charge by mobile ions in an electrolyte.
A negatively charged elementary particle.
Energy released when an electron is added to an isolated gaseous atom or molecule, using the energy-release convention.
The tendency of a bonded atom to attract electron density toward itself.
A substance whose atoms all have the same proton number.
The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
A reaction that absorbs heat at constant pressure (ΔH > 0).
A thermodynamic state function defined as H = U + PV.
Enthalpy change when a specified amount of solute dissolves in a solvent under stated conditions.
A thermodynamic state function related to energy dispersal and the number of accessible microscopic states.
At a given temperature, the product of equilibrium activities raised to their stoichiometric powers, divided by the corresponding reactant product.
An organic compound containing the group R–C(=O)–O–R′.
Escape of molecules from the surface of a liquid into the vapour phase.
A reaction that releases heat at constant pressure (ΔH < 0).
Separation of suspended solids from a fluid by passing it through a porous medium.
Energy is conserved; ΔU = q + w, where w is work done on the system.
An atom or group of atoms responsible for characteristic chemical reactions in an organic compound.
An electrochemical cell that converts energy from a spontaneous redox reaction into electrical energy.
A thermodynamic state function G = H − TS; at constant temperature and pressure, a spontaneous process has ΔG < 0.
At equal temperature, effusion rates of gases are inversely proportional to the square roots of their molar masses.
A vertical column of the periodic table.
Time required for the amount of a decaying substance or a specified reactant to fall to half its initial value.
Position and momentum cannot both have arbitrarily small uncertainties: ΔxΔp ≥ ℏ/2.
The enthalpy change of a reaction depends only on initial and final states, not the reaction pathway.
A family of organic compounds with the same functional group and successive members typically differing by –CH₂–.
Electrons occupy degenerate orbitals singly with parallel spins before pairing, for the usual ground-state filling rule.
A bonding model combining atomic orbitals on one atom to form hybrid orbitals.
Interaction with water, such as solvation of ions by water molecules.
A compound containing only carbon and hydrogen.
An attractive interaction involving hydrogen bonded to an electronegative atom and an electron-rich acceptor; it may be intra- or intermolecular.
A chemical reaction involving bond cleavage or transformation by water.
A model gas obeying PV = nRT, with negligible particle volume and intermolecular interactions.
A solution whose components obey Raoult's law throughout the composition range.
A substance that changes a visible property, usually colour, in response to a chemical condition.
Reaction rate at a particular instant, obtained from a derivative with respect to time.
Attractive and repulsive interactions between molecules or other particles.
An atom or group of atoms with a net electric charge.
Electrostatic interactions between an ion and a polar molecule.
Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
Crystals made of ions held together primarily by electrostatic interactions.
An effective measure of an ion's size in a specified chemical environment.
Minimum energy required to remove an electron from an isolated gaseous atom or ion in its ground state.
A reaction whose reverse is negligible under the specified conditions.
One of two or more compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures or spatial arrangements.
Atoms of the same element having different neutron numbers.
The SI unit of energy, equal to one newton metre.
An organic compound with a carbonyl group bonded to two carbon atoms.
A model explaining gas properties through the motion and collisions of particles.
In ordinary chemical reactions in a closed system, total mass is conserved to excellent approximation.
At equilibrium, activities satisfy the equilibrium expression; for elementary reactions, rate laws follow the reacting species' molecularity.
Chatelier's principle An equilibrium system responds to a disturbance in a direction tending to oppose that disturbance.
An electron-pair acceptor.
An electron-pair donor.
The reactant consumed first according to reaction stoichiometry, determining the maximum product yield.
A phase that flows like a liquid while retaining some directional or positional molecular order.
Attractions arising from correlated fluctuations in electron density, present between all atoms and molecules.
Ultraviolet hydrogen spectral transitions ending at n = 1.
The quantum number mℓ specifying the projection of orbital angular momentum.
The total number of protons and neutrons in a nucleus.
An instrument that separates and detects ions according to their mass-to-charge ratios.
Material that has mass and occupies space.
Temperature at which solid and liquid coexist in equilibrium at a specified pressure.
Crystals in which metal atoms are held together by metallic bonding.
A physical combination of substances with variable composition.
Amount of solute in moles divided by mass of solvent in kilograms.
Mass per mole of specified entities, commonly expressed in g mol⁻¹.
Volume per mole of a substance at stated temperature and pressure.
Amount of solute in moles per litre of solution; also called amount concentration.
The SI unit of amount of substance, containing exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ specified entities.
Amount of a component divided by the total amount of all components.
Crystals made of molecules held together by intermolecular interactions.
A formula giving the actual number of atoms of each element in a molecule.
An ion formed by electron removal from or addition to a molecule without fragmentation.
An electrically neutral entity consisting of more than one atom bonded together.
An acid–base reaction; for aqueous strong acids and bases, hydrogen and hydroxide ions form water.
An electrically neutral particle present in most atomic nuclei.
A solution that deviates from Raoult's law.
A process that is not thermodynamically favourable in the stated direction under specified conditions.
The small, dense central region of an atom containing protons and usually neutrons.
A defined electron path in historical models such as the Bohr model, not a trajectory in modern quantum mechanics.
A one-electron wavefunction; its squared magnitude gives the electron probability density.
The sum of the exponents of concentration terms in an experimentally determined rate law.
The study of carbon compounds, especially those with carbon–carbon and carbon–hydrogen frameworks.
Loss of electrons or increase in oxidation number.
The formal charge assigned to an atom by treating bonds according to electron-assignment rules.
A species that causes oxidation by accepting electrons and is itself reduced.
A separation technique using paper as a stationary support and a moving solvent.
The contribution of a gas component to total pressure; for an ideal mixture, pᵢ = xᵢP.
A fraction multiplied by 10⁶; the basis, such as mass or volume, must be specified.
Infrared hydrogen spectral transitions ending at n = 3.
No two electrons in an atom can have the same four quantum numbers.
Actual yield divided by theoretical yield, multiplied by 100%.
A horizontal row of the periodic table.
Infrared hydrogen spectral transitions ending at n = 5.
Negative base-10 logarithm of hydrogen ion activity; approximately −log[H⁺] in dilute solutions when concentration is in mol L⁻¹.
A physically homogeneous part of a system with uniform intensive properties.

A bond arising from sideways overlap of orbitals, with a nodal plane containing the internuclear axis. pKᵥ (pKw) Negative base-10 logarithm of the ionic product of water, approximately 14 at 25 °C. pKₐ Negative base-10 logarithm of the acid dissociation constant. pOH Negative base-10 logarithm of hydroxide ion activity.
A measure of how easily an electric field distorts the electron distribution of a species.
A substance composed of macromolecules built from repeating structural units.
Streams of positive ions produced in a gas discharge and observed passing through a perforated cathode.
An insoluble or sparingly soluble solid formed from a solution.
The quantum number n, identifying an electron shell and related to orbital energy and size.
A positively charged particle in the atomic nucleus; H⁺ denotes a hydrogen ion in acid–base chemistry.
Values describing allowed quantum states; for an atomic electron these are n, ℓ, mℓ and mₛ.
For an ideal solution, the partial vapour pressure of a component equals its mole fraction times its pure-component vapour pressure.
The proportionality constant in a rate law at specified conditions.
Change in reaction extent per time, or the corresponding stoichiometrically normalized concentration change per time at constant volume.
A substance consumed in a chemical reaction.
A gas whose behaviour deviates from the ideal gas law.
A reaction involving both oxidation and reduction.
A species that causes reduction by donating electrons and is itself oxidized.
Gain of electrons or decrease in oxidation number.
The fraction or percentage of atoms of an element represented by a particular isotope.
The average atomic mass relative to one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom; dimensionless.
In planar chromatography, distance travelled by a component divided by distance travelled by the solvent front from the origin.
A reaction that can proceed in both forward and reverse directions.
An ionic compound consisting of cations and anions.
A solution in equilibrium with undissolved solute at specified conditions.
A bond with electron density symmetric around the internuclear axis, often formed by head-on orbital overlap.
The equilibrium amount of solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent or solution at specified conditions.
A component dissolved in a solvent.
A homogeneous mixture of two or more substances.
The component of a solution that dissolves the solute, often present in greater amount.
Separation by distributing a solute between two phases, commonly immiscible liquids.
A distribution of radiation intensity or another measured quantity as a function of wavelength, frequency or energy.
The electron spin projection quantum number mₛ, with values +½ or −½.
A thermodynamically favourable process under specified conditions; it need not occur rapidly.
Electrode potential relative to the standard hydrogen electrode, with species in standard states at a stated temperature.
Enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms forms from an element in its standard state.
Enthalpy change when one mole of a substance burns completely in oxygen under standard-state conditions.
Enthalpy change when one mole of a compound forms from its elements in their reference states under standard-state conditions.
Enthalpy change per mole of water formed by acid–base neutralization under specified standard conditions.
For gases, IUPAC convention is 273.15 K and 100 kPa; an older convention uses 101.325 kPa.
A property depending only on the state of a system, not the path taken to reach it.
Quantitative relationships among reactants and products in chemical reactions.
Direct transition from solid to gas without passing through the liquid phase.
Everything outside the thermodynamic system that can interact with it.
The portion of the universe selected for study.
A measure of thermal state that determines the direction of spontaneous heat transfer.
Maximum product amount predicted from balanced reaction stoichiometry and the limiting reactant.
The study of heat and enthalpy changes associated with chemical and physical processes.
Determination of an analyte amount by adding a measured quantity of a reagent of known concentration.
An element whose atom has an incomplete d subshell or that forms cations with an incomplete d subshell.
A repeating structural unit that generates a crystal lattice by translation.
A hydrocarbon containing at least one carbon–carbon multiple bond.
Distillation at reduced pressure, allowing liquids to boil at lower temperatures.
Electrons in an atom that participate or can participate in chemical bonding.
Waals equation A real-gas model: (P + an²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT, with parameters for attraction and excluded volume.
Pressure exerted by a vapour in equilibrium with its condensed phase at a stated temperature.
Water incorporated in the crystal structure of a hydrate in definite proportions.
An acid that ionizes only partially in a specified solvent.
A technique for examining ordered structures by measuring the diffraction of X-rays.
The amount of product obtained or predicted in a chemical reaction.
A species carrying positive and negative formal charges while having zero net charge.
